To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
10.4 % of unselected breast cancer cases from Trinidad and Tobagohave a deleterious mutation in one of three genes (BRCA 1, BRCA 2, or PALB 2).
the prevalence of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations in breast cancer patients from the nation of Trinidad is 9 % (24 of 268) and that of PALB2 mutations is 0.75 % (2 of 268).

we identified 28 mutations in 268 breast cancer patients from the Caribbean island of Trinidad and Tobagoto, including 10.4 % of patients with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations and an additional 1.1 % of patients carrying mutations in PALB2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevalence of mutations of the BRCA1, the BRCA2, PALB2, genes among breast cancer patients in the nation of T and T.
the prevalence of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations among breast cancer patients in a Caribbean population.
the prevalence of BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations in breast cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prevalence of deleterious mutations in the genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 among breast cancer patients in the population of Trinidad and Tobego is 10.4 % (95 % CI 6.8-14.0 %).
the prevalence of mutations among the three genes in the study population was 10.4 % and the three genes were responsible for 10.4, 3.74, and 0.75 % of the cases, respectively.
the BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 mutations are common in Trinidad and Tobagans with a high prevalence of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
10.4 % of the breast cancer patients had a mutation in a breast cancer susceptibility gene and that these patients should be offered genetic counseling.

the prevalence of deleterious mutations in the three breast cancer susceptibility genes in our study population is higher than the prevalence of these mutations in other populations of African ancestry.
we have identified a high frequency of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations among breast cancer patients in a population with a high incidence of breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of mutations among breast cancer patients in this population is higher than that reported in other Caribbean populations, including the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, and Jamaica.
the prevalence of mutations is high enough that all patients in Trinidad and the Caribbean should be offered testing for these three susceptibility genes.
the burden of BRCA mutations is high in Trinidad and Tobango, and genetic testing for BRCA mutations in this population should be offered to all patients.
